response: There is limited and conflicting evidence regarding the "July effect" in patients undergoing major cancer surgery. Some studies suggest that the quality of care and patient outcomes may be compromised during the summer months when new residents start, while others have found no significant difference in outcomes. However, a 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of Surgical Oncology found no significant association between the month of admission (July vs. non-July) and postoperative mortality or complications in patients undergoing major cancer surgery. Overall, the current evidence does not strongly support the existence of a "July effect" in major cancer surgery.
